White Hat — Facts and data: what is actually here?
Red Hat — Intuition and feeling: what does this project make you feel?
Black Hat — Caution: what are the risks or gaps?
Yellow Hat — Optimism: what is the potential?
Green Hat — Creativity: what else could this become?

digm-553/assignments/asn-5-—-final-prese.title: Final Presentation

It is: here is how the encounter with tools/materials changed the inquiry. The process is part of the work. The presentation must make the invisible labor, decisions, pivots, and transformations visible.
Entry point — What was your driving curiosity? What was your dog?
The matter-network — What tools/materials were you entangled with?
Impasses and pivots — What resisted? What did that reveal?
The work — Demonstration/documentation of the project
Formative forces — How did the encounter with tools/materials change the inquiry?
Open questions — What does this work open that it doesn't answer?
Recorded presentation with demonstration. 12–15 minutes.Documentation (slides, video, or equivalent) submitted to Blackboard. Revised Speculative Proposal also due this week.

digm-553/threads/physical-digital-entang.title: Physical-Digital Entanglement
digm-553/threads/physical-digital-entang.description:
The interweaving of physical materials, bodies, and environments with digital systems. Not an interface between two separate domains — an entanglement in which each shapes the other.The signal chain at the center of this course — body → sensor → microcontroller → protocol → software → output — is not a pipeline that converts physical reality into digital representation. It is a series of transformations, each of which amplifies something and reduces something else. The body that touches the capacitive sensor is not the same as the threshold-crossing event the sensor registers. The OSC message is not the gesture. Something is always gained; something is always lost. What matters is knowing which something — and making that choice deliberately.Magnusson: the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three layers are active at once. The hardware has physical affordances that shape how you hold it, where you put it, what it can touch. The firmware has temporal properties that shape the resolution and latency of the response. The software has representational assumptions that shape what the data means. None of these layers is neutral; together they constitute the instrument.This thread tracks how physical and digital forces meet, condition each other, and produce something neither could alone — across your hardware choices, your material selections, your installation environments, and your audience's bodies.Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97, Week 103 At each arrow in your signal chain, what is being amplified and what is being reduced? Is that tradeoff intentional — a design decision — or accidental? What does your system not know about the body it's sensing? And what creative or critical work can happen in that gap? Where in your practice does the physical environment shape the digital behavior — and vice versa? Can you design the entanglement rather than just inheriting it? What material are you touching with your sensors or microcontrollers? What cultural, social, or political charge does that material carry — and does your system acknowledge it?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools*4 — on instruments as material-electric-symbolic systems and the phenomenology of digital tool relations.
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality*3 — on the thickness and materiality of digital objects; the matter-network.

digm-553/threads/making-public.html.title: Making Public
digm-553/threads/making-public.html.description:
Rendering work public is not the delivery of results. It is a continuation of the research — a way of making the formative conditions and processual transformation of the work available for encounter.Loveless, working through Haraway, argues that research-creation carries an obligation to render research public — not as a finished product submitted to evaluation, but as a practice in itself. What gets made public is not just the artifact but the forces that formed it: the impasses, the enabling constraints, the entanglements, the tools and their reductions. This is why the Final Presentation in this course is not a showcase. It is a rendering.The distinction Loveless makes is between transparency (showing your work) and accountability (taking responsibility for what your work does in the world — including what it can't do, what it excludes, and who it speaks to or past). Accountability requires knowing the stakes of the work, not just the process.For experimental media practice, making public also means confronting the question of audience: who is this for? What does it ask of the people who encounter it? A TouchDesigner patch sent to a hard drive is not public; the same patch running in a gallery space with bodies moving through it is. The difference is not technical. It is relational — and designing that relation is itself a creative and ethical act.Week 67, Week 97, Week 114 What would it mean to make your process public — not just your result? What would you have to show that you've been hiding? Who is the audience for your work, and what does it ask of them? Have you designed that ask, or inherited it from the format? Loveless distinguishes transparency from accountability. Where in your practice are you being transparent (showing your method) without being accountable (owning what the work does or fails to do)? What form is your work made public in, and what does that form assume about who can access it?
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog*3 — on the obligation to render research public, curiosity as method, and the boundary object.

digm-553/threads/research-creation.html.title: Research-Creation
digm-553/threads/research-creation.html.description:
The methodology holding critical inquiry, technical exploration, and creative production together as co-constitutive practices — not sequential phases, but registers of the same act.Manning & Massumi locate research-creation at the prebifurcation point: the moment before thinking and making diverge into separate institutional structures. At that point, making is already thinking-in-action, and conceptualization is a practice in its own right. The problem research-creation names — and refuses — is the communication model: the assumption that you research first, then make something that delivers the results.The alternative is conditioning over framing. Rather than setting up a question and then answering it, you bring co-causes into interaction and stay open to what emerges. This requires what Manning & Massumi call techniques of relation — structural devices for catalyzing interaction between forces that wouldn't otherwise meet. They are not content-specific; they transfer across disciplines and practices.For this course, the implication is practical: the Critical Technical Journal is not documentation of a separate making process. The making is not an illustration of the thinking. They interpenetrate — or the work isn't research-creation.Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97, Week 103, Week 114 Where in your workflow do making and thinking happen in the same moment — not sequentially, but simultaneously? Can you locate that moment and work from it deliberately? What would it mean for your project to be conditioned rather than framed? What are you holding open, and what are you predetermining? If you had to say what your practice is thinking right now — not what you're making, but what the act of making is already processing — what would you say? What institutional structures (program requirements, evaluation criteria, submission formats) separate your thinking from your making? How do you work inside those structures without simply reproducing them?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — the foundational text. Propositions 0–3 define research-creation, enabling constraints, and techniques of relation.
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog*3 — on curiosity as a legitimate research methodology; what it means to follow a question rather than test a hypothesis.

digm-553/threads/failure-as-method.html.title: Failure as Method
digm-553/threads/failure-as-method.html.description:
Failure and impasse are not obstacles to the project. They are data about the project — revealing the formative conditions, hidden assumptions, and structural tensions that define what the work is actually doing.Agre's concept of the hassle is foundational here: not a one-time crash, but a recurring friction — something that keeps happening at the same point in your workflow, for reasons you can't quite name. Hassles are worth writing down. They are the system telling you something structural about the gap between how your tool models the world and how the world actually works.The move Agre names — and this course practices — is to treat impasse as an intellectual resource. When something fails repeatedly, don't just fix it and move on. Ask: what assumption was I making that this failure is disconfirming? What was I treating as settled that isn't? These are the questions the Critical Technical Journal is built to hold.Manning & Massumi's concept of immanent critique is also relevant here: failure, encountered from inside the practice, reveals the pressure points of the system. You can't see those pressure points from outside. You find them by building, hitting walls, and noticing where the resistance is structural rather than incidental.Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97 What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a one-off problem, but something that keeps coming back? What is that hassle about? What assumption does it keep bumping against? When you hit a dead end in a project, how do you usually respond? Do you route around it, sit with it, or abandon it? What would it look like to study it instead? What's the difference between a failure that tells you something and one that doesn't? How do you tell them apart in the moment? If you had to name your most productive creative failure — the one that most changed how you work — what would you call it? What intermediation term would Agre give it?
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice*5 — the source of the hassle concept and the method of treating recurring friction as intellectual data.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — immanent critique as the practice of finding pressure points from inside the system.

digm-553/threads/collective-practice.htm.title: Collective Practice
digm-553/threads/collective-practice.htm.description:
The studio is not a collection of individual practices happening in parallel. It is a site of collective becoming — where techniques of relation between practitioners are themselves a subject of inquiry.Manning & Massumi describe the seminar or studio event as a kind of experiment: "For an 'event' to be an event, it is necessary that a collective thinking process be enacted that can give rise to new thoughts through the interaction on site." The condition: the potential for what might occur cannot be pre-reduced to "the delivery of already-arrived-at conclusions." This course is structured with that in mind. The critique, the potluck, the studio session — these are not performances of finished thinking. They are techniques of relation in the Manning & Massumi sense: devices for catalyzing interaction between practices at the level of their creative force.Critique, in this frame, is not judgment. It is activation — a practice of attending carefully to someone else's work in order to surface what it is doing that it may not know it's doing. A good critique question doesn't evaluate ("this works / this doesn't"). It opens ("what is this committed to? what does it refuse? what would it look like to follow that refusal further?").Collective practice also carries an ethic: you are responsible for what you bring to the room. Your presence, your attention, and your honest response to others' work are contributions to a shared intellectual environment. This is not a soft requirement. It is part of the assessment.Week 29, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97, Week 114 What is the difference between a critique that evaluates and one that activates? What does an activating question sound like? What do you bring to the room as a practitioner that no one else does? What does the collective gain from your specific presence and perspective? When you encounter someone else's work in critique, what is your first instinct — to assess it, to identify with it, to question it? What would it mean to attend to it before doing any of those things? How does your practice change when it's in dialogue with others? What has a peer's question or response revealed to you about your own work?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — on the studio event as a site of collective thinking, and techniques of relation as a domain of practice.

digm-553/threads/epistemic-tools.html.title: Epistemic Tools
digm-553/threads/epistemic-tools.html.description:
Tools are not neutral. Every instrument encodes a worldview — a set of propositions about what the world is, what can be known about it, and who that knowledge is for.Magnusson, drawing on Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, argues that instruments don't merely follow theory — they often determine it, because "instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." An epistemic tool is any instrument understood this way: as a knowledge-making artifact with its own claims built in.Ihde identifies three modalities of how instruments mediate between body and world: embodiment relations (you act through the tool, which recedes), hermeneutic relations (the tool produces data you must interpret), and alterity relations (you engage with the tool as a quasi-other). These aren't fixed categories — any practice oscillates between them, and the shift matters.Every tool also performs an amplification-reduction: it amplifies certain features of the world and systematically reduces others. The danger isn't reduction itself — all tools must reduce. The danger is when the reduction becomes invisible, when it gets naturalized into what Latour calls a black box: an object whose internal contingency has disappeared through repeated use. Fluency closes black boxes. The critique foot of Agre's split identity keeps reopening them.Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58 What does your primary tool amplify — what becomes easy, visible, measurable? And what does it reduce — what disappears, gets rounded off, or can't be represented? Who designed the defaults in your software? What assumptions about bodies, practices, and contexts are baked into those choices? Which of Ihde's three modalities describes your relationship to your tool right now? When does it shift — and what triggers the shift? What's the most naturalized tool in your practice — the one you've stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened that black box?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools*4 — the source text for the concept; covers Ihde's modalities, amplification-reduction, and the techne/episteme distinction.
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice*5 — on computational imperialism, the split identity, and the practice of making the invisible assumptions of tools visible.

digm-553/threads/entanglement.html.title: Entanglement
digm-553/threads/entanglement.html.description:
Practitioner, tool, and material do not interact as pre-formed, separate entities. They are mutually constituted through the practice itself. You don't bring a self to a tool — the self that acts is partly made by the act.Barad's posthumanist performativity replaces interaction (between pre-existing things) with intra-action (the process through which distinct agencies emerge). An apparatus — for Barad, any material-discursive arrangement that makes knowledge possible — doesn't just measure or represent phenomena; it participates in producing them. The researcher, the instrument, and the phenomenon are all co-constituted through the apparatus.For this course, that means: you are not a stable subject using a neutral tool to study an external object. You are entangled with your hardware, your software, your materials, and the site of your practice. These entanglements are not metaphors — they are structural features of how knowledge gets made. Documenting them honestly is part of what the Critical Technical Journal is for.Camus & Vinck extend this into digital materiality: the digital is not immaterial. It is made of matter — servers, cables, electricity, screen light. Every "digital" thing has a thickness, a weight, a set of dependencies. The click is a material event. The file is an inscription on physical media. Recognizing this thickness is how you stop treating your tools as transparent windows onto some other reality.Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97 What are you entangled with in your current project — not just using, but mutually constituted by? What would change about the project if that entanglement changed? Barad replaces "interaction" with "intra-action." What's the difference? Try to locate an intra-action — a moment where the boundaries between you, your tool, and your material were genuinely unclear. Where does the "digital" in your practice have material weight — consume power, require infrastructure, produce heat, leave traces? If your apparatus (the whole material-discursive arrangement of your practice) is not just measuring phenomena but helping produce them — what phenomena is yours producing?
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality*3 — on the thickness of digital objects; the materiality of inscription and infrastructure.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — the concept of co-causality and conditioning is entanglement in practice.

digm-553/threads/enabling-constraints.ht.title: Enabling Constraints
digm-553/threads/enabling-constraints.ht.description:
A limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction. The paradox at the heart of creative practice: the right constraint doesn't close things down — it opens them.Manning & Massumi's example: gravity is an implacable constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Add horizontal momentum, and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." Remove gravity and there's no arc — no lift, no landing, no jump as an event. The constraint is generative because of its resistance, not despite it.The enabling constraint is how this course thinks about everything from protocol choices to assignment structures. The MPR121 sensor's 12-point reduction is a constraint; it enables a certain kind of sculptural thinking. OSC over UDP dropping packets is a constraint; it forces a real-time compositional response to instability. The 3-hour seminar session is a constraint; it enables a depth of engagement that 50-minute sessions preclude.The critical move: distinguishing a constraint that merely limits from one that enables. Manning & Massumi: "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone." An enabling constraint is always a co-cause — it only becomes enabling in relation to something else it can push against.Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 87 What in your practice functions as gravity — the implacable resistance you push against? Is it enabling or merely limitative? What would it take to make it enabling? What's the difference between a rule you've been given and a constraint you've designed? Have you ever designed a constraint for yourself that actually worked? When you hit a wall in a project, is it usually a limitative constraint (stop here) or an enabling one (find the co-cause)? How do you tell the difference in the moment? What would it mean to design the constraints of your project before you design its content?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — Propositions 0–3; the concept of enabling constraints and conditioning is developed here in full.

digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.title: Hardware and Software Inventory
digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
"The digital system is material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." — Magnusson, Sonic Writing You could read this note as a checklist of tools we'll be using this term. But given what we've spent W01A and W01B establishing — that tools are epistemic, that instruments condition what can be thought, that amplification is always also reduction — we can't do that with a straight face.This is an epistemic inventory. For each element of the course toolkit, we're asking: what does this tool make possible, what does it foreclose, and why did we choose it?The physical-digital entanglement at the center of this course runs through a specific signal chain:Body / Material World ↓ MPR121 Sensor (capacitive touch) ↓ Adafruit QT Py RP2040 (microcontroller) ↓ CircuitPython (embedded code) ↓ OSC / UDP (protocol over Wi-Fi) ↓ TouchDesigner / Max/MSP / Ableton (host software) ↓ Sound, Image, Data Output Each arrow in this chain is a transformation — and each transformation amplifies something and reduces something. Understanding that chain, point by point, is what W01C is about.The QT Py RP2040 is a small microcontroller board built around the Raspberry Pi RP2040 chip. It runs CircuitPython — a version of Python designed for embedded systems with limited memory and no operating system.Why this board, epistemically?The QT Py is small enough to embed in an object, a garment, or a physical installation — it is not a "computer at a desk." This changes the relationship between the body and the computation. The computation moves toward the body rather than the body moving toward the computation. This is a design decision with consequences for what kind of physical-digital entanglement is possible.It also has explicit constraints: limited memory, no file system (without an SD card), no display, no persistent storage across power cycles. These are enabling constraints — they push you toward thinking about computation as a real-time process happening in a physical context, not a processing pipeline running on a workstation.Ihde's modalities here: In typical use, the microcontroller operates in a hermeneutic relation — it produces data (sensor readings) that you then interpret in software. But as your fluency develops, it can shift toward an embodiment relation, where the hardware/body interface recedes and you're thinking directly in terms of interaction rather than data.The MPR121 detects electrical conductance at 12 separate electrode points. When a conductive object (a finger, a body part, water, conductive thread, foil, fruit) comes near or touches an electrode, the sensor registers a change in capacitance.Epistemic specifics:The MPR121 models the world as twelve discrete contact points with threshold values. It does not model pressure, velocity, texture, or gesture in any richer sense. This is a substantial reduction — and a generative constraint.What this reduction enables: you have to build gestural richness out of combination, sequencing, timing, and creative use of what "electrode" means materially. The sensor touching a piece of copper tape embedded in a textile is not the same experience as touching a pad on a breakout board — even though the electrical signal may be identical.The sensor does not care about the materiality of what it touches. That indifference is the limitation. Making that indifference expressive is the research-creation challenge.Somax2 parallel: IRCAM's Somax2 system works with a similar epistemological structure at a different scale — it models musical input as sequences of symbolic events, reducing the richness of live performance to labeled categories that can be used to drive improvisation. The reduction enables the machine to respond; but the quality of the musical interaction depends entirely on how thoughtfully the reduction was designed. Same principle applies here.CircuitPython is Python stripped down for embedded environments. The key constraint: no concurrency, no threads, single-threaded event loop. Your code runs top to bottom, repeatedly, in a tight main loop.Epistemic consequence: You cannot think about this system the way you think about desktop software. There is no background thread listening for events while the foreground does something else. Everything is sequential. This forces a particular model of time — one that is actually closer to how musical performance works (step by step, no stopping) than how most software development works.The loop structure also makes the code's relationship to time explicit. The latency between sensing and responding is determined by how much work you do in each loop iteration. You feel computation as time.OSC is a protocol originally designed for real-time communication between musical instruments and software. It uses the UDP networking protocol, which means messages are sent in discrete packets that can arrive out of order or not at all — the protocol prioritizes low latency over guaranteed delivery.Epistemic framing: OSC messages have a specific structure: an address pattern (like /sensor/touch/1) and typed arguments. This structure makes the musical/physical origin of the data visible in the data itself. Unlike MIDI, which was designed around keyboard-and-note-number logic, OSC is relatively free — the address namespace is whatever you define. You are naming the world as you instrument it.The UDP choice (vs. TCP) is itself an argument about what matters: latency matters more than reliability. For real-time physical interaction, a dropped packet is usually less harmful than a 50ms delay. This is a design philosophy embedded in the protocol.TouchDesigner is a node-based visual programming environment developed by Derivative, used widely for real-time visual performance, interactive installations, and physical computing. It receives OSC messages, processes them in a dataflow graph, and routes the results to visual, audio, or other outputs.Epistemic specifics:TouchDesigner models the world as a cooking system — operators (nodes) either cook (update their output) or don't, based on whether their inputs have changed. This is a specific model of reactive computation — one that is very good for real-time visual work and less natural for sequential or text-based logic.The node-based paradigm also has an epistemological consequence: your decisions are made visible as connections. You can see the shape of your logic. This is different from writing code, where the structure of your reasoning is embedded in syntax. In TouchDesigner, the architecture is the code.The defaults matter here (returning to Magnusson): the built-in operators in TouchDesigner assume certain things about color, resolution, framerate, and timing that reflect the tool's origins in VVVV and cinema-influenced real-time graphics. When you use those defaults without questioning them, you're making an implicit argument about what your work should look like.Max/MSP is the older cousin of TouchDesigner — a node-based environment with deeper roots in algorithmic music composition and signal processing. Where TouchDesigner is GPU-native and optimized for visual output, Max is CPU-native and optimized for audio, MIDI, and data.Why both? The choice between TouchDesigner and Max is not purely technical — it is partly a question of disciplinary genealogy. TouchDesigner comes from the VJ / visual performance world; Max comes from the electroacoustic music world. They carry different assumptions about what a "performance" is, what "real-time" means, and what relationship between software and body is natural.Using both is an opportunity to feel those differences in your body as you work.The Zoom H5 is a portable, mid-range field recorder. Four inputs (two XLR combo jacks, plus the built-in capsule capsule pair), 24-bit/96kHz recording, small enough to carry anywhere.Epistemic framing: The H5 models the world as microphone placements and headroom. Unlike software recording, field recording asks you to solve problems in space and time before you can solve them in software. You can't EQ a bad room placement. The recorder forces decisions about where you are and where the sound is in a way that a software sampler does not.The H5 is also a tool for practice-based research: documentation, listening, locating yourself in a sonic environment. Used as a research tool (not just a production tool), it is a way of attending to a space before you decide what to make there.Here is the exercise this note is preparing you for:Do your own epistemic inventory. Pick three tools you already use in your practice — any tools, not necessarily the ones listed here. For each one: What does it amplify? (What becomes easy, visible, measurable?) What does it reduce? (What disappears, becomes invisible, gets rounded off?) What world does it assume exists? (What is the implicit model of activity, interaction, body, material that its design encodes?) Who designed those assumptions, and for what context? This exercise is the foundation of your ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal). It begins this week. Signal chain — the full sequence of transformations from physical world to digital output; each link is a reduction/amplification pair OSC (Open Sound Control) — a real-time messaging protocol that allows physical sensors and software to communicate; address-based, free-form namespace Capacitive touch — detection of electrical conductance changes; models touch as threshold-crossing events at discrete electrode points Cooking system — TouchDesigner's model of reactive computation; operators update only when inputs change Default assumptions — the inherited worldviews encoded in software's standard settings and built-in abstractions For CircuitPython + MPR121 + OSC → TouchDesigner: Adafruit CircuitPython documentation
MPR121 CircuitPython library
TouchDesigner OSC In CHOP documentation MicroOSC library for CircuitPython (see course repo) The signal chain described above isn't hypothetical — it's the system running in ongoing research on physical-digital entanglement and Afrofuturist sonic sculpture. These examples show the same epistemic questions operating at research scale, which is also what the course is pointing toward.The setup: Capacitive touch electrodes embedded in a sculptural hair object. A QT Py RP2040 reads the MPR121, sends OSC messages over UDP to a Max/MSP patch, which triggers sound and visual responses based on which electrodes are touched and in what sequence.The epistemic problem: The sensor models touch as 12 threshold events. But the sculpture is about touching Black hair — a gesture that carries enormous social, political, and intimate charge. The sensor cannot feel what that touch means. The gap between what the electrode reads (conductance shift at electrode 7) and what the audience experiences (touching something they were never supposed to touch) is not a technical failure. It's the piece.What this teaches: The reduction is not a bug. Choosing what the system does and doesn't know is a design decision that carries epistemological and political weight. Agre: the computer is "about" the site in its design. This sculpture asks: what is a capacitive sensor about when the electrode is hair?The enabling constraint: Because the MPR121 only reads 12 points, all gestural richness must be built at the audience and material level — through the choice of object, the installation context, the social meaning of the gesture. The hardware's reduction enables the cultural work.The setup: When building the OSC namespace for the MPR121 → TouchDesigner pipeline, you have to decide what to call the data. Options: /sensor/capacitive_threshold_event/channel/7 — too technical, reveals the measurement mechanism /presence_of_hand/right/index — too phenomenological, claims more than the sensor knows /sensor/touch/7 — intermediate; legible to both the body and the system The lesson: Every time you name a data stream, you are doing what Agre calls intermediation — choosing a level of abstraction that can bridge the phenomenological (what the interaction feels like) and the technical (what the hardware actually detects). Bad intermediation produces systems that are either uninterpretable (pure tech-speak) or dishonest (claiming the machine "knows" things it doesn't).For students: Your first OSC schema is a philosophical document. What you choose to name your data channels reveals what you think the interaction is.The setup: Somax2 (IRCAM) is an AI music improvisation system. It ingests musical input — typically MIDI or audio — models it as sequences of labeled events, and generates responsive output based on learned patterns. It "listens" and "responds," but it does so by reducing live performance to labeled categories it can reason about.The epistemic parallel: Somax2 does at the level of musical grammar what the MPR121 does at the level of touch. It models the world reductively so that the machine can act within it. The quality of the musical interaction isn't determined by how "intelligent" the model is — it's determined by how well the reduction was designed relative to the human performer's practice.Agre's "computational improvisation" angle: Agre mentioned a system operating as "an experiment in computational improvisation; rather than constructing a plan that it then executes wholesale." Somax2 is this literally. The question it raises: what does it mean to improvise with a system that knows your patterns but not your intentions?For students: When you build a system that responds to sensor input — in TouchDesigner, Max, or anything else — you are building a Somax2. You are deciding what the system knows and doesn't know. That decision is compositional, not just technical.The setup: Field recording before or alongside installation development. The H5 goes into a space — a barbershop, a kitchen, a corridor — and captures the sonic environment before any design decisions are made.The epistemic function: The H5 forces you to solve problems in space and time before you can solve them in software. Bad mic placement can't be fixed with EQ. The recorder requires you to attend — to listen, to be in the space, to commit to a position. This is the embodied, pre-digital step of research-creation.Magnusson's hermeneutic → embodiment shift: In the field, the H5 starts in an embodiment relation (you act through it, attending to what the mic hears). When you bring recordings back to the studio, it shifts to hermeneutic (you now interpret what was captured, what it means, what it missed). The shift is where research-creation happens: the difference between what the recorder heard and what you remember hearing is your first research question.For students: What would it look like to do a listening session in the space where your project will live, before you touch any software? The H5 exercise (or any field listening practice) is the answer.

digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.title: Epistemic Tools Introduction
digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
"Instruments have a life of their own. They do not merely follow theory; often they determine theory, because instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." — Hankins & Silverman, quoted in Magnusson If W01A established research-creation as the methodological orientation of this course, W01B establishes the epistemic status of the tools you work with. These two moves are connected: if making is already a mode of thinking, then the instrument you make with is already shaping the kinds of thought that are possible.This is what Magnusson, following Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, means by epistemic tools: instruments are not passive implements waiting to be used — they are active participants in the construction of knowledge. The choice of instrument is not neutral. It conditions what questions you can ask, what results you can produce, and — eventually — what you consider beautiful, interesting, or true.This puts tool choice in a new light. Choosing TouchDesigner over Processing, Max/MSP over SuperCollider, a capacitive sensor over a camera — these are not just technical decisions. They are epistemological ones.Don Ihde identified three phenomenological modalities of instrument-use — three ways that instruments mediate between the body and the world:You act through the instrument, which extends your body or amplifies your senses. The instrument recedes into the background — you experience through it, not at it. A well-practiced keyboard player doesn't think about the keys; they think about the music. The keys are an extension of the hand.The instrument produces data that you must interpret. A spectrograph, a heat map, an oscilloscope reading. The instrument mediates reality by translating it into a representation — but that representation requires interpretive work to become knowledge.The instrument becomes something you engage with for its own sake — as a quasi-other, a presence with its own agency. Virtual reality headsets, interactive installations, or a generative system that responds to you all produce this kind of relation. You are not acting through them; you are with them.Important: These modalities are not exclusive categories — they are tendencies. Any given practice involves mixtures and oscillations between them. And they are not value-neutral: each modality shapes what you notice, what you miss, and what you expect the instrument to do for you.Ihde's most directly practical insight: every instrument involves amplification-reduction transformations. It amplifies certain features of the world and reduces others. There is no exception to this.A microphone amplifies pressure-wave events in a certain frequency range and reduces everything else. A MIDI controller amplifies discrete pitch/velocity events and reduces continuous, gestural sound. A capacitive touch sensor amplifies conductivity at specific points and reduces everything that isn't electrical contact.The danger is not that tools reduce — they have to. The danger is forgetting that they do. When the reduction becomes invisible, the thing not being captured disappears from your thinking entirely.Magnusson on software: Musical software encodes inherited defaults: equal-tempered tuning, temporal quantization, note-based event models. These are not facts about music — they are contingent historical choices that have been naturalized. They have become what Latour (and Bowker & Star) call black boxes.A black box is an object or system whose internal workings have become invisible through repeated use. Latour: objects "establish themselves as black boxes through repeated use and in the process their origins disappear."Bowker and Star extend this: "the more naturalized the object becomes, the more unquestioning the relationship of the community to it; the more invisible the contingent and historical circumstances of its birth, the more it sinks into the community's routinely forgotten memory."Notice what this means for practice: the tools you're most fluent with are the most dangerous. Fluency produces blindness. The instrument you've used for years is the instrument whose assumptions you've most thoroughly absorbed into your practice without noticing.CTP connection (Agre): This is why the "split identity" matters — one foot in craft, one foot in critique. The craft foot needs fluency. The critique foot needs to keep opening the black boxes that fluency keeps closing.Agre's phrase names a specific version of this: computers "aim to reinvent virtually every other site of practice in its own image." They are built from representational models of the activities they will be used in. But they don't just represent — they restructure.A digital audio workstation doesn't just record and edit audio. It restructures the practice of making music around the concept of a timeline, discrete regions, channels, effects chains, automation curves. These aren't neutral containers — they are a model of music-making built by engineers with particular assumptions about what music is. "A computer, then, does not simply have an instrumental use in a given site of practice; the computer is frequently about that site in its very design." This is why Agre says that technical people often experience phenomenological texts as "sounding like mysticism." The mismatch isn't in the philosophy — it's that the computer's representational model and the phenomenologist's model of experience are genuinely incommensurable. You can't translate one into the other because they aren't the same kind of thing. Agre's solution: stop translating, start learning on their own terms.Magnusson frames the historical problem this way: Western philosophy has long separated techne (making, craft, technique) from episteme (knowledge, theory, science). Instruments of art were not instruments of knowledge; skill was not wisdom.This separation is now being productively challenged — by cognitive science (embodied cognition, enactivism), by STS (Science and Technology Studies), by research-creation methodology, and by practitioners in new interfaces for musical expression, interactive art, and critical making.The instruments become epistemic — fusing instrument with composition, as in the work of Gordon Mumma, David Tudor, or more recently in live-coding and instrument design. The digital system is, as Magnusson puts it, "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three registers are active at once.Three questions to hold as you work through this course:What does your tool amplify? What aspects of your practice does it make easier to see, hear, measure, or manipulate?What does your tool reduce? What is systematically missing from what your tool captures? What can't it represent — and how has that shaped what you've been making?Who designed the reduction? The defaults in your software were chosen by someone with specific assumptions. What were those assumptions, and whose experience of the world did they take as universal?These aren't rhetorical. They are the starting points for your Critical Technical Journal (ASN 2). Epistemic tool — an instrument that is a knowledge-making artifact; tools determine what is possible and thus what can be thought Embodiment / hermeneutic / alterity relations — Ihde's three phenomenological modalities of instrument-world relationship Amplification-reduction — every tool amplifies certain features and reduces others; no tool is neutral (Ihde) Black box — a naturalized object whose internal contingency has become invisible through repeated use (Latour, Bowker & Star) Computational imperialism — the tendency of computing to reinvent every site of practice in its own representational image (Agre) Techne / episteme — the historically-separated domains of craft-knowledge and theoretical-knowledge, now being rejoined Magnusson — Epistemic Tools4 (Ch. 3, selected sections)

digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.title: Research-Creation as Method
digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
"Making would already be thinking-in-action, and conceptualization a practice in its own right." — Manning & Massumi, Thought in the Act Most of what we call "research" and most of what we call "creative practice" assume they are separate activities. Research produces knowledge. Practice produces work. The knowledge informs the work. The work illustrates the knowledge. This is the institutional model — and it's the model we're going to spend the rest of this course systematically inhabiting and turning.Research-creation is the term Manning & Massumi use for the activity that occurs at what they call the prebifurcation point — before research and creation diverge into institutional structures that evaluate them by separate criteria. At that point, making and thinking are not distinct acts. They are two registers of the same act, happening simultaneously.The theme of Week 01 is "Practice Immanent Critique." Here's what that phrase means from the ground up.An immanent critique does not stand outside a system to pass judgment. It works from inside — inhabiting the structure, understanding its logic from within, and then finding the pressure points where it might be turned. Manning & Massumi's definition: "An immanent critique engages with new processes more than new products, from a constructivist angle. It seeks to energize new modes of activity, already in germ, that seem to offer a potential to escape or overspill ready-made channelings into the dominant value system. The strategy of immanent critique is to inhabit one's complicity and make it turn — in the sense in which butter 'turns' to curd." Notice what this requires: inhabiting complicity. You are not exempt from the system you critique. You work within it, on its tools, in its institutions, using its grants and its grades. Immanent critique means doing that while turning it — not waiting until you're free of it to begin.For this course: We are working at a university. We use tools (TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, Ableton, Python) that carry embedded worldviews. We receive grades. All of this is our complicity. Immanent critique is the method by which we make that complicity productive rather than just reproductive.Manning & Massumi acknowledge a tension: the institutional framing of research-creation — especially in the context of digital media — pushes it toward "formatting artistic activity for more directly economic forms of delivery to stakeholders." Digital media gets funded in part because it "employs the same technological platforms as the increasingly computerized economy."This is not a contradiction that resolves. It's an ongoing friction. The work is to neither ignore this friction nor be paralyzed by it — but to treat it as what Agre would call a hassle: a recurring friction that is itself data about the structure of the field.The danger Manning & Massumi identify: research-creation "settles into a communication model revolving around the delivery of results." The goal instead is what they call "an interpenetration of processes rather than a communication of products."What does that mean in practice? When you work on a project in this course, you are not primarily building something that will be assessed. You are practicing something — developing a relationship to your tools, your materials, and your questions — and the artifact is the record of that practice, not the point of it.These are technically different acts. Framing is setting up a structure: here are the rules, here are the constraints, here is the question, go. Conditioning is bringing co-causes into interaction such that something emerges that neither cause alone would produce. "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone… Emergent process, dedicated to the singular occurrence of the new, agitates inventively in an open field. Programmed organization, on the other hand, functions predictably in a bounded frame and lends itself to reproduction." In this class, we are going to try to condition rather than frame — including how we structure the class sessions themselves. We set up initial conditions; we don't predetermine outcomes.The concept that connects all of this: enabling constraints.An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect even though it may be limiting in its form. The classic example: gravity is a constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Without gravity to push against, there is no arc, no lift, no landing. The jump is a collaboration between the dancer and gravity — two co-causes whose interaction produces something neither does alone. "In our experience, unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects." This applies directly to the hardware and software in this course. The MPR121 sensor constrains what counts as input. CircuitPython constrains what you can compute on the microcontroller. OSC protocol constrains the format of the data. These are not obstacles — they are the material conditions out of which something emerges. The question is not how to eliminate constraints but how to turn them from limitative to enabling.Manning & Massumi introduce the concept of techniques of relation: "devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction" that comprise "a domain of practice in their own right."Techniques of relation are not content — they don't depend on what you're making. They are structural — they shape how things interact, how processes co-evolve, how different elements of a practice can be brought into productive contact. They operate in two modes: Techniques that set up initial conditions — propitious starting points for emergence Techniques that modulate an event as it moves through its phases — improvised steering without predetermined destination A key property: "Techniques as we understand them do not depend exclusively on the content of the practices but move across their respective processes at the site of their potential multiplication." A technique is transferable. It can move from sound to movement to code to pedagogy.Assignment connection: Part of your ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal) practice is to identify the techniques of relation already operating in your practice — and to begin consciously designing new ones.If every practice is already a mode of thought, what is your current practice thinking?Manning & Massumi open Thought in the Act with: "Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act. To dance: a thinking in movement. To paint: a thinking through color. To perceive in the everyday: a thinking of the world's varied ways of affording itself."So: to program — a thinking in what? To route audio signals — a thinking in what? To touch a capacitive sensor — a thinking in what? To capture field recordings — a thinking in what?These are not rhetorical questions. Your first journal entries will begin to answer them. Research-creation — activity at the prebifurcation point where making and thinking are co-constitutive, not sequential Immanent critique — inhabiting complicity and making it turn; critique from inside, not outside Enabling constraint — a limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction Conditioning — bringing co-causes into interaction toward open, emergent outcomes (vs. framing toward predetermined ones) Techniques of relation — devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction; transferable across practices Manning + Massumi — Thought in the Act8 (Propositions 0–3, pp. 83–94)

digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
Private instructor synthesis. Not published. Use to prep seminar voice, discussion pivots, and live examples.High Level:
Manning & Massumi argued that "research-creation" is actually a way of refusing the institutional separation between thinking and making — treating the act of practice itself as the site where concepts are generated, not just applied.Dissertation Level:
In my current work — whether it's the sonic sculpture series or the Somax2 sessions — this explains why I hit the impasse of feeling like the "intellectual" work (reading, writing the proposal) and the "technical" work (building the hardware/software system) were happening in separate rooms. I was assuming they were supposed to meet at the end (delivery of results) rather than interpenetrating the whole time. The dissertation chapters I've been struggling to write are stuck because I'm framing, not conditioning. I need to let the making speak, not just illustrate.Lab Level:
Students need to care about this because their projects will be stale unless they stop treating the "concept part" and the "build part" as sequential phases. If you're doing your research first and then making the thing that illustrates it, you're not doing research-creation. The build IS the research. The question is how to make that visible in documentation.
"What is your practice thinking right now? Not what are you making — what mode of thought is already active in the act of making it?"
"Where in your current workflow do you experience the split between 'I'm working' and 'I'm thinking'? Can you locate the exact moment?"
"Manning & Massumi say: 'unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects.' What in your practice functions as gravity — as the enabling resistance you need?"
The Don't Play in My Hair sculpture is a useful live example of enabling constraints. The capacitive sensor grid on the hair sculpture doesn't interpret touch. It detects threshold crossings at electrode points. That reduction — from the full richness of touching someone's hair (texture, pressure, temperature, social charge) to a binary event at 12 points — is both a loss and a condition. The sculpture works because the machine can't feel what the touch means. The gap between what the sensor reads and what the human feels is the piece.This is what conditioning looks like: two co-causes (the sensor's reductive model, the culturally charged act of touching Black hair) brought into interaction. Neither cause alone produces the meaning. The interaction is the work.High Level:
Agre argued that "critical technical practice" is actually a way of sustaining a split identity in research — one foot in building, one foot in critiquing — such that the work is always already reflecting on its own assumptions, not saving that reflection for a separate paper.Dissertation Level:
In my work with Somax2 and sensor-based systems, this explains why I kept hitting the impasse of: "my technical experiments produce things, but I don't know how to write about them in a way that doesn't sound like either a user manual or a philosophical abstraction." That was the sign of the split identity not working. Agre's "intermediation" is the move I was missing — developing a vocabulary at the middle level of abstraction that bridges the phenomenological (what it feels like to play with Somax2) and the technical (what Somax2 actually does). The term I've been building toward — "transducing Black epistemologies" — is an intermediation term. It's neither fully technical nor fully philosophical.Lab Level:
Students need to care about this because without the split identity, the Critical Technical Journal (ASN 2) becomes either a build log or a theory essay — and neither is what it's supposed to be. The journal works when the craft voice and the critique voice talk to each other in the same entry. You need both feet on the ground.
"What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a crash, not a one-time failure — but something that happens again and again? That's your first hassle. Write it down."
"Agre says his breakthrough was learning phenomenological philosophy 'on its own terms, not as a spec.' What would it mean to learn your current software stack on its terms — not what it can do for you, but what it's about?"
"If your tools 'reinvent every site in their own image' — what image is your favorite tool reinventing the world as?"
The OSC message schema I designed for the MPR121 sensors — /sensor/touch/[channel] — is an intermediation term. It's not called /capacitive_threshold_event (too technical) and it's not called /presence_of_hand (too phenomenological). "touch" is a middle-level abstraction that's legible to both the body and the system. Every time I name a data stream in OSC, I'm doing intermediation.The hassle I hit repeatedly: OSC over UDP drops packets when the Wi-Fi is contested. Latency spikes. The sensor responds, the software doesn't, and the interaction feels broken. This is a system hassle — a recurring friction that tells me something structural about the setup. The intermediation question: what's the right name for this impasse? Not "packet loss" (too technical) and not "the system feels dead" (too vague). Maybe: "the signal arrives but the presence doesn't."High Level:
Magnusson argued that "epistemic tools" is actually a way of recognizing that when you pick up an instrument — any instrument — you're not just picking up a functional object but adopting a set of propositions about what the world is and what can be known about it.Dissertation Level:
In my work, this explains the recurring tension between the Zoom H5 and my DAW. The H5 models my research sites as "mic placements in a room with specific gain staging." The DAW models them as "audio files at specific sample rates." Neither model is the sonic event I'm trying to capture — the presence of a space, the resonance of an object, the social charge of a material. The tool I'm using is always making a claim about what matters about sound. Part of the dissertation project is to make that claim explicit, contested, and productive — which means writing about the tools, not just with them.The Zoom as epistemic tool: it has an embodiment relation in the moment of recording (I act through it, attending to what the mic hears), but the files it produces immediately shift into a hermeneutic relation (I have to interpret what the recording means, what it captures and doesn't). Recognizing that shift is part of how I document practice.Lab Level:
Students need to care about this because unless they can articulate what their tools claim about the world, they can't critique that claim — and their projects will just reproduce the assumptions of the default software without knowing it. "I used Ableton" is not a methodology statement. "Ableton models time as a horizontally-arranged grid of discrete regions, and I'm testing what happens when I treat that grid as a material resistance rather than a container" — that's a methodology statement.
"Pick one button on your hardware or one default setting in your software. Who decided that was the default? Why?"
"The MPR121 sees the world as 12 threshold events. What does it not see? What would need to change for it to see that?"
"Magnusson says the digital system is 'material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control.' Which layer are you spending the most time in? Which are you ignoring?"
In Sun Ra Cryosleep and Buffalo Soldier, the firmware on the microcontroller is doing the same basic work — reading sensor state, sending OSC messages — but the meaning of the touch events is entirely different. The circuits are the same; the epistemic framing is different. This is the clearest demo I can offer of Magnusson's point: the tool (the MPR121 + RP2040) is the same; but the instrument — the thing that makes meaning from the tool — is built by the design around it, the materials it touches, the cultural context it operates in.The hardware doesn't know it's touching Black hair. The intelligence is in the entanglement: sensor + material + audience + context + installation design. The epistemic tool is the whole configuration, not just the chip.Ask: "What are you complicit in right now? Not rhetorically — concretely. What system are you working inside of right now that you didn't choose?" Wait. Let it sit. Someone will say: Drexel. Someone will say: their laptop. Someone will say: Western music. All correct.Draw the split on the board. Put "writing the proposal" on one side and "building the thing" on the other. Ask: "Where does thinking happen?" Most point to the proposal side. Then: "But when you're building, what are you doing?" Let them find the word: thinking. Then erase the line.Return to the Woodland Gloss question: "What is this sensor claiming about the world?" Pull back to epistemics. The setup guide is for outside of class; the seminar is for this question."What's the electrode in your DAW? What's the thing that converts the world into your system's native representation? Start there."
Manning & Massumi's enabling constraint ↔ Agre's hassle — both are framings of productive friction; one is generative, one is diagnostic. A hassle, worked carefully, can become an enabling constraint.
Magnusson's black box ↔ Agre's computational imperialism — both describe what happens when a tool's assumptions become invisible and self-perpetuating.
Manning & Massumi's conditioning ↔ Magnusson's amplification-reduction — conditioning is the practice; amplification-reduction is the mechanism. You condition by choosing which reductions are generative.
Agre's split identity ↔ Manning & Massumi's prebifurcation point — the split identity is required precisely because institutions keep pulling the two feet apart. R-C is the attempt to stay at the prebifurcation point as long as possible.

For context, these are two authors who think that the form of writing itself should enact the argument being made; so it is written as such. It also may read as a bit “overly critical,” but it is important to understanding the context of their work. Let the reading wash over you once. Then read it again more slowly, with a highlighter or notebook.On the first pass: Mark any sentence that feels like it's writing about your own practice, even if you can't yet say why. Don't worry about the vocabulary.On the second pass: Look for these three things specifically: The word technique and how they're using it The distinction between conditioning and framing Any moment where they talk about what a body does (including a digital body) These are not quiz questions! Where is that point in your current practice? Is there a moment in your workflow when the thinking and the making are still the same thing? When does the split happen? They distinguish between framing a project (setting up a structure in advance) and conditioning one (bringing co-causes into interaction so something can emerge). Think of a project you've worked on. Was it framed or conditioned, maybe even both, at different stages? What did that feel like from the inside? "An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect, even though it may be limiting in its form." What enabling constraints are already active in your tools, materials, and methods? digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
Due: Week 02 - Bring your contribution to class. This is part of ASN 1: Potluck + Speculative Proposal4.The (Im)material Potluck is a collective opening ritual for the course. Each student brings one thing — physical or immaterial — to contribute to a shared conversation about material, tools, and practice. It is as much a show-and-tell as it is an opening proposition.Consider the object you bring is an argument. It says something about your practice, your research, your questions. Your job is to be able to articulate what argument yours is making. Your contribution can be physical or immaterial, hence (im)material. What it cannot be is arbitrary. It should be something with stakes for your own work.Physical examples: A material you keep returning to (fabric, copper tape, wood, clay, wire) A piece of hardware that has shaped how you think (a sensor, a circuit board, a connector, an old device) An object from your research environment (something from a site you've been working in) A tool that frustrates you in productive ways Immaterial examples: A dataset, protocol, or schema you work with A sound or sound file (something you've recorded or that recurs in your practice) A constraint or rule you've imposed on yourself An image, a diagram, a piece of notation A system or process (something that has no single physical form) If your contribution is immaterial, come ready to share it on screen/speakers or describe it precisely. Vagueness is not the same as immateriality.For each contribution, you'll have a few minutes to speak (~5min). Prepare to address:1. Why this thing? Not its origin story — the practical reason it has stakes in your work. What does this object or material make possible in your practice that other things don't? What does working with it feel like, and what does that feeling tell you? 2. What does it open? What questions does it raise that you can't yet answer? What does it put into contact with other things in your work? Where does it lead?3. What is it thinking? Manning & Massumi: "Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act." Objects and materials are part of practices: they aren't passive. What mode of thought is already active in the thing you're bringing? What does it do to the practice it's part of — not just what you do with it, but what it does to you? You don't need fully formed answers. You need to have asked the questions and be willing to sit with them in the room.The reading assigned this week is useful preparation for how to think about your object before you bring it. A few entry points:Manning & Massumi: They distinguish between framing (setting up a structure in advance) and conditioning (bringing co-causes into interaction to produce emergence). Is your object a frame or a condition? What does it enable that you didn't design in advance? There is no size or format requirement. One thing is enough. If it's fragile, pack accordingly. If it's large, photograph it and bring the photo plus a fragment. If it's truly immaterial and screen-sharing is difficult, prepare a 30-second verbal description precise enough that the room can hold it. You will not be graded on the quality of the object, only on the specificity and honesty of how you speak about it (plus your reflection post on it as well! ).

See Readings10 for full citations.Week 11Tools are not neutral. Every instrument encodes a worldview — a set of propositions about what the world is, what can be known about it, and who that knowledge is for.Magnusson, drawing on Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, argues that instruments don't merely follow theory — they often determine it, because "instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." An epistemic tool is any instrument understood this way: as a knowledge-making artifact with its own claims built in.Ihde identifies three modalities of how instruments mediate between body and world: embodiment relations (you act through the tool, which recedes), hermeneutic relations (the tool produces data you must interpret), and alterity relations (you engage with the tool as a quasi-other). These aren't fixed categories — any practice oscillates between them, and the shift matters.Every tool also performs an amplification-reduction: it amplifies certain features of the world and systematically reduces others. The danger isn't reduction itself — all tools must reduce. The danger is when the reduction becomes invisible, when it gets naturalized into what Latour calls a black box: an object whose internal contingency has disappeared through repeated use. Fluency closes black boxes. The critique foot of Agre's split identity keeps reopening them.
Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58 What does your primary tool amplify — what becomes easy, visible, measurable? And what does it reduce — what disappears, gets rounded off, or can't be represented? Who designed the defaults in your software? What assumptions about bodies, practices, and contexts are baked into those choices? Which of Ihde's three modalities describes your relationship to your tool right now? When does it shift — and what triggers the shift? What's the most naturalized tool in your practice — the one you've stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened that black box?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools*4 — the source text for the concept; covers Ihde's modalities, amplification-reduction, and the techne/episteme distinction.
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice*5 — on computational imperialism, the split identity, and the practice of making the invisible assumptions of tools visible.
Research-Creation36   Enabling Constraints20   Entanglement26   Physical-Digital Entanglement21   Failure as Method26Epistemic ToolsA limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction. The paradox at the heart of creative practice: the right constraint doesn't close things down — it opens them.Manning & Massumi's example: gravity is an implacable constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Add horizontal momentum, and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." Remove gravity and there's no arc — no lift, no landing, no jump as an event. The constraint is generative because of its resistance, not despite it.The enabling constraint is how this course thinks about everything from protocol choices to assignment structures. The MPR121 sensor's 12-point reduction is a constraint; it enables a certain kind of sculptural thinking. OSC over UDP dropping packets is a constraint; it forces a real-time compositional response to instability. The 3-hour seminar session is a constraint; it enables a depth of engagement that 50-minute sessions preclude.The critical move: distinguishing a constraint that merely limits from one that enables. Manning & Massumi: "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone." An enabling constraint is always a co-cause — it only becomes enabling in relation to something else it can push against.
Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 87 What in your practice functions as gravity — the implacable resistance you push against? Is it enabling or merely limitative? What would it take to make it enabling? What's the difference between a rule you've been given and a constraint you've designed? Have you ever designed a constraint for yourself that actually worked? When you hit a wall in a project, is it usually a limitative constraint (stop here) or an enabling one (find the co-cause)? How do you tell the difference in the moment? What would it mean to design the constraints of your project before you design its content?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — Propositions 0–3; the concept of enabling constraints and conditioning is developed here in full.
Research-Creation36   Epistemic Tools14   Entanglement26   Failure as Method26   Physical-Digital Entanglement21Enabling ConstraintsPractitioner, tool, and material do not interact as pre-formed, separate entities. They are mutually constituted through the practice itself. You don't bring a self to a tool — the self that acts is partly made by the act.Barad's posthumanist performativity replaces interaction (between pre-existing things) with intra-action (the process through which distinct agencies emerge). An apparatus — for Barad, any material-discursive arrangement that makes knowledge possible — doesn't just measure or represent phenomena; it participates in producing them. The researcher, the instrument, and the phenomenon are all co-constituted through the apparatus.For this course, that means: you are not a stable subject using a neutral tool to study an external object. You are entangled with your hardware, your software, your materials, and the site of your practice. These entanglements are not metaphors — they are structural features of how knowledge gets made. Documenting them honestly is part of what the Critical Technical Journal is for.Camus & Vinck extend this into digital materiality: the digital is not immaterial. It is made of matter — servers, cables, electricity, screen light. Every "digital" thing has a thickness, a weight, a set of dependencies. The click is a material event. The file is an inscription on physical media. Recognizing this thickness is how you stop treating your tools as transparent windows onto some other reality.
Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97 What are you entangled with in your current project — not just using, but mutually constituted by? What would change about the project if that entanglement changed? Barad replaces "interaction" with "intra-action." What's the difference? Try to locate an intra-action — a moment where the boundaries between you, your tool, and your material were genuinely unclear. Where does the "digital" in your practice have material weight — consume power, require infrastructure, produce heat, leave traces? If your apparatus (the whole material-discursive arrangement of your practice) is not just measuring phenomena but helping produce them — what phenomena is yours producing?
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality*3 — on the thickness of digital objects; the materiality of inscription and infrastructure.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act*8 — the concept of co-causality and conditioning is entanglement in practice.
Research-Creation36   Epistemic Tools14   Enabling Constraints20   Physical-Digital Entanglement21   Failure as Method26EntanglementFailure and impasse are not obstacles to the project. They are data about the project — revealing the formative conditions, hidden assumptions, and structural tensions that define what the work is actually doing.Agre's concept of the hassle is foundational here: not a one-time crash, but a recurring friction — something that keeps happening at the same point in your workflow, for reasons you can't quite name. Hassles are worth writing down. They are the system telling you something structural about the gap between how your tool models the world and how the world actually works.The move Agre names — and this course practices — is to treat impasse as an intellectual resource. When something fails repeatedly, don't just fix it and move on. Ask: what assumption was I making that this failure is disconfirming? What was I treating as settled that isn't? These are the questions the Critical Technical Journal is built to hold.Manning & Massumi's concept of immanent critique is also relevant here: failure, encountered from inside the practice, reveals the pressure points of the system. You can't see those pressure points from outside. You find them by building, hitting walls, and noticing where the resistance is structural rather than incidental.
Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97 What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a one-off problem, but something that keeps coming back? What is that hassle about? What assumption does it keep bumping against? When you hit a dead end in a project, how do you usually respond? Do you route around it, sit with it, or abandon it? What would it look like to study it instead? What's the difference between a failure that tells you something and one that doesn't? How do you tell them apart in the moment? If you had to name your most productive creative failure — the one that most changed how you work — what would you call it? What intermediation term would Agre give it?

Research-Creation36   Epistemic Tools14   Enabling Constraints20   Entanglement26   Collective Practice21Failure as MethodThe interweaving of physical materials, bodies, and environments with digital systems. Not an interface between two separate domains — an entanglement in which each shapes the other.The signal chain at the center of this course — body → sensor → microcontroller → protocol → software → output — is not a pipeline that converts physical reality into digital representation. It is a series of transformations, each of which amplifies something and reduces something else. The body that touches the capacitive sensor is not the same as the threshold-crossing event the sensor registers. The OSC message is not the gesture. Something is always gained; something is always lost. What matters is knowing which something — and making that choice deliberately.Magnusson: the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three layers are active at once. The hardware has physical affordances that shape how you hold it, where you put it, what it can touch. The firmware has temporal properties that shape the resolution and latency of the response. The software has representational assumptions that shape what the data means. None of these layers is neutral; together they constitute the instrument.This thread tracks how physical and digital forces meet, condition each other, and produce something neither could alone — across your hardware choices, your material selections, your installation environments, and your audience's bodies.
Week 110, Week 29, Week 37, Week 48, Week 58, Week 67, Week 76, Week 87, Week 97, Week 103 At each arrow in your signal chain, what is being amplified and what is being reduced? Is that tradeoff intentional — a design decision — or accidental? What does your system not know about the body it's sensing? And what creative or critical work can happen in that gap? Where in your practice does the physical environment shape the digital behavior — and vice versa? Can you design the entanglement rather than just inheriting it? What material are you touching with your sensors or microcontrollers? What cultural, social, or political charge does that material carry — and does your system acknowledge it?
